extracted.intended_audience: immigration applicants, immigration attorneys/practitioners, benefits-granting agencies, and public commenters on DHS/USCIS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when an alien is a 'public charge' for inadmissibility and related immigration adjudications under DHS's proposed rule, including definitions of public charge and public benefits, program lists, monetization/duration thresholds, evidentiary approach, and exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes that a person should be considered a public charge based on the receipt of financial support from the general public through government funding (i.e., public benefits). DHS does not believe the operative definitions suggest or require a primary dependence standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses statutory and dictionary meaning (e.g., Merriam-Webster: 'one that is supported at public expense'; Black’s Law: 'an indigent; a person whom it is necessary to support at public expense by reason of poverty or illness'). Case law emphasizes dependence/support by the public; DHS focuses on receipt of public benefits as the operative measure of being a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of public benefit (monetizable and non-monetizable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public benefit includes a specific list of cash aid and noncash medical care, housing, and food programs where either (1) monetizable benefits exceed a 15 percent of Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) threshold within a 12-consecutive-month period, or (2) non-monetizable benefits are received for more than 12 months in the aggregate within a 36-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed regulatory citation: 8 CFR 212.21(b) and (c). The definition also addresses combined receipt situations (see combined threshold entry). The monetizable/non-monetizable distinction is central to determining dependence by degree and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizable benefits threshold (15 percent of FPG)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetizable benefits count toward a public benefit determination if the cumulative value of one or more such benefits that can be monetized exceeds 15 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for a household of one within a period of 12 consecutive months (based on per-month FPG for months benefits are received).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referred to as the proposed '15 percent standard or threshold.' DHS considered the 'primarily dependent' standard and other agency definitions when selecting this threshold. Monetization methodology is defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-monetizable benefits duration threshold (>12 months in 36-months)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits that cannot be monetized are treated as relevant if they are received for more than 12 months in the aggregate within a 36-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration is aggregated across a 36-month lookback (or prospective window as applicable). This threshold is intended to capture sufficient duration of non-monetizable benefit receipt to indicate dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined monetizable + non-monetizable threshold (9 months rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alien receives a combination of monetizable benefits equal to or below the 15 percent threshold together with one or more benefits that cannot be monetized, DHS proposes that the threshold for duration of receipt of the non-monetizable benefits would be 9 months in the aggregate within a 36-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combined rule adjusts the duration threshold downward when some monetizable benefits are also present, reflecting that combined supports may indicate dependence even if monetizable benefits alone do not cross 15% FPG.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of monetizable public benefits considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to consider the following monetizable benefits: any Federal, State, local, or tribal cash assistance for income maintenance (including Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), and General Assistance), and benefits that can be monetized in accordance with proposed 8 CFR 212.24 (examples listed include SNAP, Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetizable benefits are those DHS can determine a cash value for; examples and statutory citations are provided in the preamble (e.g., SNAP: 7 U.S.C. 2011–2036c; Section 8 programs: 24 CFR parts cited). Cash assistance includes transfers in the form of cash, checks, money transfers, or instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of non-monetizable public benefits considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to consider certain non-cash benefits that cannot be monetized, including nonemergency Medicaid (with specified exceptions), premium and cost sharing subsidies for Medicare Part D, benefits provided for institutionalization for long-term care at government expense, certain subsidized housing programs, benefits provided under IDEA, and benefits provided to foreign-born children of U.S. citizen parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonemergency Medicaid exclusions are explicitly noted (e.g., emergency medical conditions as prescribed in section 1903(v) of Title XIX). DHS limits the universe of non-cash benefits considered to a specific list to promote administrability and consistency across adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude transactional/value-exchange benefits (grants, contracts, licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider grants, contracts, and licensures (as defined under PRWORA) in public charge inadmissibility determinations because they are transactional/value-exchanged benefits that may involve exchange of government resources for value provided by the alien and do not necessarily evidence lack of self-sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: these benefits are not indicative of dependence; PRWORA's broad definition is therefore narrowed for public charge purposes. See discussion of 8 U.S.C. 1611(c) and PRWORA definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate individualized welfare support from general public services
rubrics_metrics.description: Only individualized public support to the needy (directed to an individual's subsistence needs) is relevant; general welfare services provided broadly to all residents from general tax funds are not generally relevant to public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Matter of Harutunian and BIA precedent distinguishing individualized welfare (relevant) from municipal/state services provided to all residents (not evidence of being a public charge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt alone does not establish likelihood of becoming a public charge; consider ability to remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien's past receipt of welfare alone does not establish that he or she is likely to become a public charge; adjudicators should weigh the alien's ability or inability to remedy past or current reliance on public welfare for financial support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Matter of Perez, Matter of Vindman, Matter of Harutunian) shows that capacity to overcome reliance is critical. Evidence of remedying reliance may overcome a ground of inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective vs. status-change determination timing
rubrics_metrics.description: For admissibility and adjustment of status, receipt of benefits is determined on a prospective basis (i.e., likely at any time in the future to receive benefits above threshold); for extension of stay and change of status applicants, the determination regarding receipt above thresholds is based on whether the alien has received since obtaining the nonimmigrant status in question, is receiving, or is likely at any time to receive benefits above the thresholds (not exclusively prospective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates how DHS applies thresholds depending on the immigration proceeding (prospective for admission/adjustment; partly retrospective for change/extension of nonimmigrant status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include both cash and a limited set of non-cash benefits for comprehensive administrability
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to consider cash benefits and a limited list of non-cash benefits because both types can indicate lack of self-sufficiency; limiting the non-cash universe promotes consistency and administrability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS recognizes indirect costs to benefits-granting agencies and seeks to provide consistency for adjudications; the limited list responds to program prevalence and taxpayer expense considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider degree and duration of dependence as a continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS recognizes 'welfare dependence' is a continuum (varying in degree and duration) and that quantifying/qualifying reliance is challenging; the proposed monetizable/non-monetizable and combined thresholds are intended to capture sufficient levels of dependence in degree and duration to sustain a finding of public charge or likelihood thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS relied on prior policy's 'primarily dependent' concept, other agency definitions, and Federal Poverty Guidelines in setting thresholds; adjudicators should consider both how much support and for how long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude certain cash assistance categories (e.g., disaster assistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all cash assistance qualifies as 'cash assistance for income maintenance' under the proposed rule; e.g., Stafford Act disaster assistance (FEMA Individual Assistance) and comparable disaster assistance from State/local/tribal governments would not be considered cash assistance for income maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other categories of cash assistance that are not intended to maintain a person at a minimum level of income likewise would not fall within the definition; adjudicators should examine program purpose when classifying cash assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical data (SIPP) and evidence limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS used the 2014 Panel of the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) to analyze participation rates; DHS acknowledges limitations (e.g., SIPP may not reflect current participation, does not distinguish current immigration classification, does not show whether receipt was authorized) and seeks comment on alternative data sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes sampling variability: estimates with relative standard error >30% are considered unreliable. DHS used annual averages and explains SIPP methodology and limitations in the preamble; commenters may provide alternative reliable data.
